reason: Every number reproduces, and the design argument behind them survives every attack I could make on it. MEASURED (chromium, 1440x960, owner-flight, pixels sampled off the real screenshot, not from CSS): on ?v=paper the field under the rail is pure white and the rail composites to rgb(167,163,242) = 2.309:1, while the .b-bar border-bottom and .b-foot border-top hairlines both composite to rgb(217,217,217) = 1.412:1 - the accent rail is 1.635x an ordinary rule. On ?v=ink the same declaration composites to rgb(48,44,123) = 1.587:1 and the same two --fore-16 hairlines composite to rgb(55,55,55) = 1.588:1. Ratio 0.999. The finding's '1.587 vs 1.588' is exact. The two ratified indigo objects verify too: .b-todayRule and .b-item[data-lead=true] .b-tick both read rgb(79,70,229) at opacity 1, 6.288:1 on paper and 3.003:1 on ink. So the rail is the only indigo on the surface that is dimmed, and it is dimmed by the same amount on the ground where indigo has 3.00:1 of total headroom instead of 6.29:1. NOT A RESTATED GATE. audit.mjs's palette lock (near(), line 61-62) compares the DECLARED rgb triple within +/-1 and never parses alpha; `opacity` is not in its colorProps list at all, so indigo at any opacity passes. Its contrast pass is text-only - it is gated on hasText and on the AA thresholds for size/weight (lines ~238, ~357) and never looks at a rule. interaction-check.mjs touches .b-rail twice: line 1556 asserts one exists, line 2121 asserts its background is non-transparent under forced-colors. Nothing on either gate measures how strong the rail is on either ground. Not in SETTLED either: accent-spent-twice-never-on-the-event is about accent=once and defends the lock's two indigo objects; this finding adds no third use, it asks the ratified third use to be keyed to its ground. NOT TASTE, AND NOT MARGINAL. Two things make it structural rather than a preference. (1) `opacity: 0.5` is the ONLY fractional opacity anywhere in b.css and shell.css - I grepped both files, the complete set of opacity values in the lab is 0.5 (once), 0 and 1. Every other tone in this master is a --fore-N token that flips with the ground by design; this one line is the single tone in the lab that does not know which room it is in, and it is the line that carries the one decision round 10 changed. (2) The lock names this exact failure class - 'A token chosen for one ground is a token that fails on the other, which is exactly how the first attempt at this left two controls painting white on white' - and 0.5 is not on the declared alpha ladder (0.90/0.72/0.62/0.46/0.28/0.16/0.10/0.06/0.04) on either side. The master's own forced-colors block already concedes the point: b.css:1550 special-cases `[data-accent="structure"] .b-rail { background: CanvasText; opacity: 1; }` - the author already knew 0.5 is too weak once the palette is not paper. THE FIX IS AN IMPROVEMENT, VERIFIED VISUALLY. I injected the proposed rules at runtime and captured the same crop at DPR 1 and DPR 2 on ink. At 0.5 the rail is a dim bruise-coloured line, visibly duller than the .b-todayRule 200px away from it; at opacity 1 it reads as a deliberate indigo spine in the same tone as the today rule, and the 9px filled lead tick still dominates it easily because hierarchy between a 1px rule and a filled dot is carried by area, not by tone. It does not become a ground: it is 1px. On paper 0.5 -> 0.46 moves 2.309:1 to 2.084:1, imperceptible, and buys a declared step. Neither gate moves: the palette lock never read the alpha, the contrast pass is text-only, and interaction-check's only rail assertion is under forced-colors where opacity is already 1. The compound selector wins as claimed - I confirmed data-ground and data-accent are both on BODY in the master, so (0,3,0) beats (0,2,0). ONE THING THE FIX GETS WRONG, sharpened below: `[data-accent="structure"] .b-rail` also paints the PAST rail. In state=day on ink I measured .b-back .b-rail at rgb(79,70,229) opacity 0.5. Unscoped, opacity:1 would put full-strength indigo down the rail of what has already happened, which directly contradicts the round-10 sentence the accent exists to make - indigo draws the part of the rail that is STILL AHEAD. The finding's own assertion already targets .b-measure:not(.b-back) .b-rail; the CSS just has to agree with it.
